title: Discovery: Nimbus Health migration from OpenAI to Dedicated
next_steps: Send SOC2 + security whitepaper and KMS integration notes
Share Dedicated pricing sheet and commit options
Run a 2-week pilot on Dedicated (2 GPU nodes) with existing prompts and eval set
Schedule technical deep dive on 2025-07-22 with Nimbus infra team
transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2025-07-15 16:00 UTC / Duration: 54m Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Daniel Ortiz (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Nimbus CTO), Liam Bates (Nimbus ML Eng), Alyssa Park (Nimbus Sec) Summary (auto): Discuss migration from OpenAI hosted to Redwood Dedicated; primary drivers are cost predictability, data residency/compliance, and latency stability. Customer concerned about eval parity, compatibility with existing vLLM/TGI stack, and KMS/SAML integration. Agreed to pilot and share security artifacts. Transcript: (0:00) Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining; quick intro, I'm Maya from Redwood, AE. Daniel's my SE, he'll handle the deep infra stuff. (0:12) Priya Singh: Hi all, Priya here, CTO at Nimbus. We've been using OpenAI for production chat, but costs are creeping and we have some latency variance. We're exploring Dedicated or Private options. (0:25) Liam Bates: Hey, Liam. I run the inference infra and the current flow is OpenAI via proxy, some prompt engineering, and we also run an internal vLLM+TGI stack for batch scoring. (0:37) Daniel Ortiz: Nice to meet you. Quick question — when you say latency variance, are we talking tail latency on short queries or big context windows? (0:45) Liam Bates: Mostly short queries, 2-4 tokens responses plus a bit of chat history. But we also have longer embeddings and some reranking where context can be 1–3k tokens. (0:57) Alyssa Park: And from security, we need encryption at rest with KMS, SAML SSO, RBAC, and SOC2/audit logs. Data residency is a must for some PHI-adjacent workflows. (1:12) Maya Chen: All good — Redwood Dedicated covers KMS integration, SSO/SAML, and we support private control plane options for VPC. We have compliance docs; happy to share SOC2 and our KMS patterns. (1:24) Priya Singh: How about model compatibility? We rely on the same prompts tuned for OpenAI gpt-4o — will we get parity on Dedicated? (1:36) Daniel Ortiz: Great question — parity depends on model choice. If you use one of the same family models we host (or a verified variant), we run through an eval parity process. For customers migrating, we typically run your eval set through our infra to measure output deltas and latency. We also have quantization/precision knobs; sometimes there's a small shift in responses when switching quantization. (1:58) Liam Bates: We're also using vLLM locally for some offline stuff and TGI for an internal endpoint. If we move workload to Dedicated, can we reuse our TGI/vLLM artifacts or weights? (2:12) Daniel Ortiz: You can bring model weights in many cases; for private/on-prem deployments we support typical formats. For Redwood Dedicated (hosted in our infra dedicated to you), we onboarding models from model hubs or you can use our catalog. For vLLM/TGI parity, we do kernel/serving optimizations that can change perf profile but we validate functional equivalence with your tests. (2:36) Priya Singh: Any customers who came from OpenAI and saw identical eval scores? (2:42) Maya Chen: We've had a few — generally we see <3% change on core NLU tasks after tuning runtime configs and sometimes mapping to the closest model variant. We document each delta. We can run your eval set as a POC to show exact numbers. (2:58) Liam Bates: That'd be good. Also concerned about inference cost — OpenAI pricing is per-token; what does Dedicated look like? (3:07) Maya Chen: Dedicated is reserved capacity. Pricing wise you commit to nodes (GPUs) and it's amortized; effective per-token cost often drops for high throughput, and you get stable latency SLOs. We'll share a pricing sheet — cost depends on batch sizes, sequence lengths, and caching. (3:24) Alyssa Park: About data retention — if we use Dedicated, is customer data retained in logs? Auditability is important. (3:31) Daniel Ortiz: By default, tenant data is isolated; we can disable persistent logs or configure retention. Audit logs are available for admin actions. For PHI workflows we recommend Private (VPC or on-prem) and we can provide a private control plane. (3:48) Priya Singh: For timeline, we want to pilot in Q3, internal stakeholders are product and infra. Success criteria: parity on top-10 prompts, <50ms median latency for short queries, and lower 95th percentile latency than current. Also a target to reduce per-request cost by 30% if possible. (4:10) Daniel Ortiz: Sounds reasonable. Quick technical — what's your current request volume, qps, and token distribution? (4:18) Liam Bates: Peak 150 qps across endpoints, average 70 qps. Token distribution mostly 16-64 tokens on chat, and some embedding bursts. (4:27) Daniel Ortiz: For those numbers Dedicated with 2 A100-ish nodes should be a comfortable starting point; we can autoscale burst with Dedicated burst pool. You'll want prefix/KV cache set up for chat to reduce tokens. (4:43) Priya Singh: The cache — does Redwood support prefix caching and partial KV cache reuse for chat sessions? (4:51) Daniel Ortiz: Yes, we have automatic KV caching and prefix cache for recurrent conversation patterns; it's configurable per-route. That tends to cut token compute significantly. (5:05) Liam Bates: Regarding integration — we use SSO (Okta), and internal infra is in AWS us-east-1. Any network constraints? (5:13) Maya Chen: Dedicated can be deployed in cloud regions; for Private we can spin up a VPC peering option, and we also have an on-prem package if needed. SSO via SAML/Okta is supported. (5:25) Alyssa Park: Do you have a documented security checklist for legal/procurement? We need encryption in transit and at rest, KMS integration, key rotation, and SOC2/ISO certs. (5:36) Maya Chen: Absolutely — we'll send our security pack with SOC2 reports, pen test summary, and KMS integration docs. We'll also include our data residency options. (5:46) Priya Singh: One thing — we previously attempted a vLLM-based local deployment and hit some memory/kv cache issues on long context. How does Redwood handle KV cache sizing and memory pressure? (5:59) Daniel Ortiz: Our serving runtime manages KV cache retention per session and evicts by policy. For long contexts we stream KV across shards and we have techniques to keep memory bounded. We can show telemetry in Redwood Console for cache hit rates. (6:19) Liam Bates: Nice. Any mention of function-calling parity? We rely on structured output for actions. (6:25) Daniel Ortiz: We support function/tool calling and structured outputs; for Dedicated we can expose the same endpoints with streaming responses and toolhooks. (6:34) Priya Singh: On governance, how do you handle model rollouts and automatic fallbacks? If a new version regresses on our prompts, do you offer A/B or automatic fallback? (6:45) Maya Chen: Yes — Redwood Console supports canary rollouts, A/B, and automatic fallback to a previous model or to a cheaper tier. We tie eval regressions to alerts if your golden prompts fail thresholds. (6:57) Liam Bates: Good. For pilot sampling — we want to re-run our eval harness across current OpenAI outputs and Redwood Dedicated outputs. Do you have tooling to import our evals? (7:07) Daniel Ortiz: We can ingest your eval set as CSV or a simple JSONL format, run batch evaluations, and produce side-by-side metrics. We'll send the evaluation template. (7:16) Priya Singh: About latency numbers — you mentioned 50ms median is possible. For our stack, current median is about 80ms. What levers get us to 50ms? (7:27) Daniel Ortiz: The main levers are dedicated GPU with optimized kernels, short context batching, and keeping a hot KV cache. Also choosing lower latency model variants and tuning quantization profiles helps. There's always tradeoffs with quality. (7:43) Priya Singh: Speaking of quality — how do you communicate small generation diffs to product teams? We need to avoid user-facing regressions. (7:51) Maya Chen: We typically run a smoke evaluation and produce diff reports with examples. We can add human-in-the-loop checks on critical prompts. We can also freeze a model version per route during a rollout. (8:05) Liam Bates: On the topic of bring-your-own-model (BYOM) — if we bring a TGI-exported model, do you handle conversion and quantization?
(8:14) Daniel Ortiz: Yes, we have onboarding pipelines for common formats; we also provide recommended quantization profiles. For very custom kernels you may need a bit of tuning but we help. (8:26) Priya Singh: Are there any known regressions when moving from OpenAI to open models you host? (8:33) Maya Chen: Mostly small style or tokenization differences. Function-calling semantics can differ slightly; hence the eval step. We log examples and offer rollback. (8:44) Alyssa Park: For contractual SLAs — Dedicated includes latency SLOs and uptime commitments? (8:50) Maya Chen: Yes, Dedicated comes with SLA tiers for uptime and defined latency targets; specifics vary by commitment level. (8:58) Liam Bates: Cool. Procurement question — what does onboarding look like timeline-wise for a pilot? (9:04) Maya Chen: Typical pilot gets you from sign-off to first tests in 1–2 weeks: security review, account setup, model onboarding, and running evals. For Dedicated we provision nodes which can take a bit longer if we need specific regions. (9:18) Priya Singh: Great. Can you share a reference for a healthcare customer who did a Dedicated migration? (9:24) Maya Chen: I can check — we have anonymized case studies and can make an intro under NDA. (9:31) Liam Bates: One more technical: do you support local inference endpoints to minimize egress when we have on-prem data? (9:39) Daniel Ortiz: For Private/on-prem deployments yes; for Dedicated we can set up VPC with peering to limit egress. (9:47) Priya Singh: Ok — sounds like we should run the eval and cost comparison. Questions from security team will be handled after we get the doc pack. (9:55) Maya Chen: Next steps recap: we'll send SOC2/security pack, pricing + commit options, evaluation template, and proposed pilot config. Also schedule a tech deep dive on 7/22. (10:08) Priya Singh: Thanks. One ask — include example telemetry from Redwood Console so infra can see cache hit rates and token breakdown. (10:17) Daniel Ortiz: Will do, we'll include dashboard screenshots and sample traces. (10:22) Alyssa Park: Also include encryption key rotation process and who has access to keys. (10:28) Maya Chen: Noted. (10:31) Priya Singh: Any blockers from our side? We'll need budgets and sign-off from procurement, but procurement usually asks for SOC2, pricing, and SLA. (10:41) Maya Chen: We'll include that in the packet. (10:45) Liam Bates: One operational thing — does Redwood provide a migration playbook for switching routes in-prod with minimal downtime? (10:54) Daniel Ortiz: Yes — we have a migration runbook: canary routing, traffic split, rollback, and metrics to watch. We'll attach that. (11:05) Priya Singh: Perfect. (11:08) Maya Chen: Anything else? (11:10) Alyssa Park: No, that covers it. (11:12) Priya Singh: Thanks all. Recap / Action Items (auto): - Redwood to send security pack (SOC2, KMS notes, encryption and key rotation) — Maya Chen - Redwood to share Dedicated pricing sheet + commit options — Maya Chen - Redwood to share evaluation template and schedule pilot start — Daniel Ortiz - Schedule technical deep dive 2025-07-22 with Nimbus infra team — Maya/Daniel End of call.
